one_line: Allen Pike (Forestwalk Labs) on why voice input with visual output beats voice-to-voice for AI now, and the latency tactics (fast small model, eager short inference turns, stable prompt prefixes) that make it feel responsive.
summary: Allen Pike argues that voice is a good input for AI but visual output is the better response channel, since current voice-in, voice-out systems feel slow and dumb. He describes a voice agent Forestwalk Labs runs inside its team calls, which acted on a request (filing a Linear issue) in about a second. The core problem is latency: full voice conversation needs roughly 200 ms, while a visual response that appears within about one second still feels seamless to the user. He reports that a small GPT-5 Mini had P95 latencies of 5 to 10 seconds, so he prefers a Haiku-class model with a latency-focused inference platform. The responding model should hand heavy work to a larger model asynchronously and interleave the results. Three practices make the loop work: a fast model with a short context, inference every one or two seconds while the user is still speaking, and a stable prompt prefix so provider prefix caching cuts cost and time. The talk is short, practitioner-level, and gives a few concrete numbers, with few specifics on architecture details.

key_ideas.idea: Voice in, visuals out is the practical pattern now
key_ideas.detail: Voice is a high-bandwidth input, but voice output is hard to get right. Visual output has a larger latency budget and can carry rich HTML, controls and illustrations, so the speaker favors it as the response channel.

key_ideas.idea: Current voice interfaces feel slow and dumb
key_ideas.detail: Most people's experience with voice assistants is poor. The speaker's view is that the problem is model speed and capability, not that speaking is a bad input.

About 100 ms feels instant, about 1 s is the limit before users lose their train of thought, and full voice-to-voice conversation needs about 200 ms or less. Visual output within about a second is within the attention span and feels seamless.

key_ideas.idea: Use a fast small model, with an async handoff for heavy work
key_ideas.detail: The real-time responder must be Haiku-class or a small open model on a latency-focused platform. Heavy reasoning goes to a larger model that runs asynchronously, and its results are interleaved back into the live session.

key_ideas.idea: Send inference eagerly while the user is still talking
key_ideas.detail: Waiting for silence wastes most of the latency budget. Sending inference every one or two seconds during speech lets the agent act on partial, mid-sentence changes.

key_ideas.idea: Keep the prompt prefix stable to use prefix caching
key_ideas.detail: If the first ~90% of each request is identical, providers can serve it from cache, which the speaker says can be up to 90% cheaper and faster. Only the final ~10% should change, and output tokens should be kept low. He applies the same rule to long-running and frequently running agents.

techniques.name: Two-tier model split (fast responder plus async thinker)
techniques.how: A Haiku-class or small open model handles the live turn with a short context. It hands off heavier work as an async message to a larger model, then weaves the result into the live conversation when it arrives.
techniques.when: Real-time voice or chat UIs where some requests need deep reasoning but the user must not wait on the reasoning.

techniques.name: Eager short-interval inference
techniques.how: Instead of waiting for end-of-speech silence, run inference every one or two seconds while the user is speaking, and let the model update its action as the utterance changes.
techniques.when: Voice turn-taking where silence detection adds seconds of latency and users revise mid-sentence.

techniques.name: Prefix-stable context layout for caching
techniques.how: Keep the first ~90% of the prompt identical across requests (system prompt, tool definitions, stable context) and append the variable part at the end. Minimise output tokens.
techniques.when: Any frequently running or long-running agent that calls a provider with prefix caching.

techniques.name: Visual response envelope
techniques.how: Answer with on-screen visuals, such as generated HTML, interactive controls or illustrations, instead of spoken audio, since the visual only needs to appear within about a second.
techniques.when: Products where the user can look at a screen and audio output would miss the ~200 ms conversational budget.

numbers.claim: Human-perceived instant response is about 100 ms; the limit before users lose their train of thought is about 1000 ms
Full voice-in, voice-out conversation needs about 200 ms latency or less
GPT-5 Mini P95 latencies of about 5000 to 10000 ms in the speaker's production use, despite being cheaper than the larger model
Inference should run every 1 to 2 seconds while the user is speaking
Prefix caching can make inference up to 90% cheaper and faster when the start of the context is unchanged
Thinking Machines demoed a model doing continuous inference in 200 ms time slices (a few weeks before the talk)

hot_takes: Voice as an AI input is controversial, but speaking is the most natural high-bandwidth channel, and the fix is latency rather than dropping voice.
Most voice assistant experiences today are both slow and dumb, and that combination is why people are down on voice input.
Voice-to-voice with novel architectures is not needed yet: voice in with visual out already lands inside the attention span.
Small cheap models are not enough for real-time voice; P95 latency is the deciding metric, and in the speaker's testing Haiku-class models beat a smaller GPT-5 variant.

relevance.why: InferCraft serves models, and the talk's point that stable prompt prefixes drive provider caching applies to the proxy and memory layers. The talk gives no measurements for self-hosted vLLM.
relevance.action: In the L1 proxy or L2A context assembly, check that the system prompt, tool schemas and retrieved memory are ordered stable-first so cached prefix hits are maximised; log cache hit rate per request.

relevance.why: ProsHarness runs long Claude Code sessions and resumes them from checkpoints. Keeping the prefix stable across resumes would help caching, but the talk does not discuss checkpoint or resume architecture.
relevance.action: Check whether checkpoint resume re-sends a changing preamble (timestamps, plan state) at the start of the prompt; move volatile content to the end so the cached prefix survives resumes.

relevance.why: The two-tier pattern (small fast model in the loop, larger model async for heavy work) and the prefix-caching rule both apply to cheap-model pipelines. The talk's latency numbers are anecdotal.
relevance.action: Prototype a two-tier entity-resolution or extraction step: a Haiku-class model answers quick triage calls on the hot path and queues hard cases to a larger model, then measure P95 and cache hit rate.
